title: Modes & Permissions
description: Plan before you poke: permission modes, Shift+Tab, and allow/ask/deny rules.

theory.title: Look before you leap
theory.body:
Kip never scuttles into a new tide pool without scouting it first. **Plan mode** is Claude Code's scouting mode: Claude reads files and runs read-only commands to explore, then proposes a step-by-step plan, but it does **not** edit your source files. Edits stay blocked until you **approve the plan**.

To start a session already in plan mode, add the `--permission-mode` flag and the mode name `plan`. Both spellings work:
`claude --permission-mode plan`
`claude --permission-mode=plan`

theory.title: Switching modes with Shift+Tab
theory.body:
Already in a session? Press `Shift+Tab` to cycle permission modes. The indicator under the prompt shows where you are:
• **Manual** (`default`): asks before edits and commands
• **accept edits** (`acceptEdits`): auto-approves file edits
• **plan** (`plan`): explores read-only and proposes a plan
There is also `bypassPermissions`, which skips prompts entirely and belongs only in containers or VMs (more next lesson).

A typical plan-mode flow: switch to plan → describe the change → Claude explores and proposes a plan → you ask questions and refine it → you approve → Claude edits → you review the diffs.

theory.title: Make plan mode the default
theory.body:
Want every session in a project to start in plan mode? Put this in the project settings file `.claude/settings.json`:
• `"permissions"` is the section for permission settings; its `{ }` holds the options.
• `"defaultMode"` is the exact key name (camelCase) for the mode sessions start in.
• `"plan"` is the value: a mode name, written as a JSON string in double quotes.

Swap the value for `"acceptEdits"` or `"default"` to start in those modes instead.

exercises.prompt: What does Claude do in plan mode?
options: Generates a plan and immediately applies it
Reads and explores, then proposes a plan without editing your source files
Edits files without asking but never runs commands
Runs every command without asking for permission
exercises.explanation: Plan mode exists so you can agree on the approach first, which is why Claude only reads and proposes while edits wait for your approval.

exercises.prompt: You are mid-session and want to switch into plan mode. What do you press?
exercises.explanation: `Shift+Tab` cycles the permission modes mid-session, so you can enter plan mode without restarting.

exercises.prompt: Match each permission mode to what it does.

pairs.right: Skips prompts; containers and VMs only

exercises.explanation: Each mode trades convenience for oversight differently, so you pick the one that matches how much you want to review.

exercises.prompt: You are in plan mode before a risky payments refactor. Which prompt is better?
options: Explore src/payments and propose a step-by-step plan to move Stripe calls behind a PaymentProvider interface. List the files you would touch and the risks; do not edit anything yet.
exercises.explanation: Naming the scope, the goal and the expected output (a plan, no edits) gives Claude a clear job for the planning phase.

exercises.prompt: Put a plan-mode workflow in order.
steps: Press Shift+Tab until the indicator shows plan mode
Claude explores the code and proposes a plan
Ask questions and refine the plan
Approve the plan so Claude can start editing
exercises.explanation: Refining and approving the plan before any edit means mistakes are caught while they are still cheap words, not code.

exercises.prompt: Make every session in this project start in plan mode.
exercises.explanation: `permissions.defaultMode` is the setting Claude Code reads at startup, so setting it to `"plan"` makes every session begin in plan mode.
exercises.hint: Pattern: "permissions": { "defaultMode": "<mode name>" }, with the mode as a quoted string.

exercises.prompt: Start a new Claude Code session directly in plan mode by typing `claude` with the permission-mode flag set to `plan`.
exercises.explanation: The `--permission-mode` flag picks the starting mode, so `plan` guarantees nothing is edited until you approve a plan.

exercises.scenario: You want to add rate limiting to the login endpoint, but you are new to this codebase. Write the prompt you would send in plan mode.
exercises.sample: I'm new to this codebase and we're in plan mode. Read @src/api/login.ts and the existing middleware in @src/middleware/. Goal: plan rate limiting for the login endpoint (5 attempts per minute per IP). Constraints: reuse an existing middleware pattern if there is one, no new dependencies, and do not edit any files yet. Done when you've given me a numbered plan listing the files to change, how to test it, and the risks.
exercises.explanation: Context, file references, a precise goal and a clear "done" let Claude return a plan you can actually approve.

lessons.title: Auto-Accept & Cycling
lessons.description: acceptEdits, Shift+Tab and the danger zone

theory.title: Auto-accept edits
theory.body:
In `acceptEdits` mode Claude Code automatically approves **file edits** and common filesystem commands such as `mkdir`, `touch`, `mv` and `cp` inside your working directory.

Other shell commands (installing packages, pushing, publishing like `npm publish`) **still ask**. It is perfect when you are iterating on code you'll review in the diff anyway. Start in it with the same flag as plan mode, just a different value. The value is case-sensitive camelCase: `acceptEdits`.

theory.title: Cycling and the danger zone
theory.body:
`Shift+Tab` moves one step each press: Manual (`default`) → `acceptEdits` → `plan`, and, when they are available, `bypassPermissions` and `auto` as well. So from Manual, one press gives accept edits and a second press gives plan. Watch the indicator under the prompt.

`--dangerously-skip-permissions` starts in `bypassPermissions`, which skips **all** permission prompts. Kip only uses it inside an isolated **container or VM**, never on a laptop with real credentials.

theory.title: Your control panel
theory.body:
Three kinds of controls, three moments:
• **Flags** pick the mode when you launch `claude`.
• **Shift+Tab** switches modes mid-session.
• `/permissions` (typed inside a session) shows and edits your allow, ask and deny rules. You'll write those rules in the next lesson.
theory.code:
claude --permission-mode default       # Manual: asks first
claude --permission-mode acceptEdits   # auto-approve edits
claude --permission-mode plan          # read-only planning
claude --dangerously-skip-permissions  # skip prompts (sandbox)

> /permissions                         # inside a session

exercises.prompt: You are in acceptEdits mode and Claude wants to run `npm publish`. What happens?
options: It runs automatically because all commands are accepted
Claude switches to plan mode first
You are still asked, since it is not a file edit or common filesystem command
exercises.explanation: acceptEdits only removes friction for file edits, so risky actions like publishing still need your explicit yes.

exercises.prompt: You start a session with `claude --permission-mode default` and press Shift+Tab once. Which mode are you in now?
exercises.explanation: Each `Shift+Tab` press moves one step along Manual → acceptEdits → plan, so one press from default lands on acceptEdits.

exercises.prompt: Match each control to its job.

pairs.right: Start a session in plan mode

exercises.explanation: Flags set the mode at launch, keys switch it mid-session, and `/permissions` manages the rules, so each control fits a different moment.

exercises.prompt: You switched to acceptEdits to do a rename. Which prompt is better?
options: Rename formatDate to formatIsoDate in src/utils/date.ts, update every import, then run npm test and show me any failures.
exercises.explanation: With edits auto-approved you review less as you go, so a precise scope and a test step are your safety net.

exercises.prompt: Where is it reasonable to use `--dangerously-skip-permissions`?
options: Anywhere, as long as you have git
Your main laptop with production credentials
A shared server everyone logs into
exercises.explanation: Skipping prompts removes your last check, so it is only safe where Claude cannot reach anything that matters.

exercises.prompt: Starting in Manual mode, walk to plan mode and then implement.
steps: Press Shift+Tab: the indicator shows accept edits
Press Shift+Tab again: the indicator shows plan mode
Ask Claude to research and propose a plan
Approve the plan and let Claude start editing
exercises.explanation: Each Shift+Tab press moves exactly one step, so from Manual you need two presses to reach plan mode.

exercises.prompt: Start a new session that automatically accepts file edits, using the permission-mode flag with the value `acceptEdits`.
exercises.hint: Pattern: claude --permission-mode <mode> (the value is camelCase: acceptEdits)
exercises.explanation: Mode values are exact names, so `acceptEdits` (camelCase) auto-approves edits from the very first turn.

exercises.prompt: You are inside a throwaway Docker container. Start Claude Code with the flag that skips all permission prompts.
exercises.explanation: The flag is named "dangerously" because it removes every safety prompt, which is only acceptable where nothing real can be damaged.

lessons.title: Permission Rules
lessons.description: settings.json allow, ask and deny lists

theory.title: Where rules live
theory.body:
Permission rules live in settings files:
• `~/.claude/settings.json` applies to **you in every project**.
• `.claude/settings.json` is the **project** file you commit so the team shares it.
• `.claude/settings.local.json` is **personal** to this project and not committed.

Inside a session, type `/permissions` to see every rule and which file it came from.

theory.title: The three lists
theory.body:
Rules go in three lists inside `"permissions"`:
• `"allow"`: runs **without asking**.
• `"ask"`: always **asks you first**.
• `"deny"`: **blocked**, never runs.

Each list is a JSON array `[ ]` of rule strings in double quotes, separated by commas. In this example tests and the docs folder are free, `git push` needs a yes, and `.env` and `curl` are off-limits.

theory.title: Rule syntax: Tool(specifier)
theory.body:
A rule is a tool name, optionally followed by a specifier in parentheses: `Tool` or `Tool(specifier)`. Tool names are capitalized: `Bash`, `Read`, `Edit`, `Write`, `WebFetch`, `WebSearch`, `Glob`, `Grep`.

• `Bash(...)` takes a command; `*` is a wildcard for "anything here". The older `:*` suffix means the same: `Bash(ls:*)` = `Bash(ls *)`.
• `Read(...)` / `Edit(...)` take a path; `./` means the project folder and `**` means any files in any subfolder.
• `WebFetch(domain:...)` takes a website domain.
theory.code:
Bash(npm run build)          exactly that command
Bash(npm run *)              npm run build, npm run test --watch
                             (but NOT npm install)
Read(./.env)                 the .env file in the project
Read(./docs/**)              everything under docs/
WebFetch(domain:github.com)  fetches from github.com

exercises.prompt: Match each settings file to who it applies to.
exercises.explanation: Splitting settings into user, project and local files lets you share team rules while keeping personal ones out of git.

exercises.prompt: Which rule matches `npm run build` but NOT `npm install`?
exercises.explanation: The `*` only replaces what comes after `npm run `, so commands that start differently, like `npm install`, do not match.

exercises.prompt: Your team wants the same allow rules for lint and tests on every machine. Where do they go?
exercises.explanation: Only the committed `.claude/settings.json` travels with the repo, so it is the one file every teammate gets.

exercises.prompt: You want Claude to configure permissions for the repo. Which prompt is better?
options: In .claude/settings.json, add allow rules for Bash(npm run lint) and Bash(npm run test *), and a deny rule for Read(./.env). Leave other settings untouched.
exercises.explanation: Naming the file, the exact rules and the boundaries prevents Claude from guessing and adding an overly broad allow.

exercises.prompt: Let Claude run test scripts and read docs freely, but never read the .env file.
exercises.explanation: Putting a rule in `allow` skips the prompt and putting it in `deny` blocks the call, so the list name decides the outcome.
exercises.hint: Rule lists are "allow" (runs freely), "ask" (confirm first) and "deny" (blocked).

exercises.prompt: Block reading .env, and let Claude fetch pages from the Python docs without asking.
exercises.explanation: The tool name before the parentheses decides what is being controlled: `Read` for file reads and `WebFetch` for web requests.
exercises.hint: Pattern: Tool(specifier). File paths go in Read(...), domains go in WebFetch(domain:...).

exercises.prompt: Inside a session, open the dialog that lists your permission rules and the file each one comes from.
exercises.hint: Pattern: / + the name of the feature (the same word as the settings section).
exercises.explanation: `/permissions` shows every allow, ask and deny rule with its source file, so you can see why something is or isn't allowed.

exercises.scenario: Ask Claude to set up a shared permissions config: tests and lint should run without prompts, .env files must never be read, and curl should be blocked.
exercises.sample: Our team keeps getting prompted for routine commands, and we need secrets locked down. Update @.claude/settings.json (create it if missing). Using the scripts in @package.json, add allow rules for Bash(npm run lint) and Bash(npm run test *). Add deny rules for Read(./.env), Read(./.env.*) and Bash(curl *). Constraints: don't change any other settings and don't add broader rules than these. Done when you show me the final file and confirm it is valid JSON.
exercises.explanation: Stating the reason, the exact rules, the file and what "done" looks like means nothing broader than intended gets allowed.

theory.title: Deny first, always
theory.body:
Rules are checked in a fixed order: **deny**, then **ask**, then **allow**. The first match decides, and how specific a rule is does not change the order. If **nothing** matches, Claude Code falls back to the current permission mode (for example, Manual asks).

So with this config, `git status` runs freely, `git push origin main` asks, and `rm -rf build` is blocked. An allow rule can never carve an exception out of a deny rule.

theory.title: Worked examples
theory.body:
• allow `Bash(git *)` + deny `Bash(git push *)` → `git push` is **blocked** (deny checked first).
• allow `Bash(npm *)` + ask `Bash(npm publish *)` → `npm publish` **asks** (ask beats allow).
• allow `Bash(aws s3 ls)` + deny `Bash(aws *)` → `aws s3 ls` is **blocked**, even though the allow is more specific.

Reminder: `Bash(ls *)` and the older `Bash(ls:*)` mean the same thing.

theory.title: Enforced, not requested
theory.body:
Permission rules are enforced **by Claude Code**, not by the model. Writing "never read .env" in `CLAUDE.md` shapes what Claude *tries*; a `deny` rule decides what is *allowed*.

A bare tool name in `deny`, like `"WebFetch"`, removes that tool from Claude's context entirely. A scoped rule like `"Bash(rm *)"` keeps the tool but blocks matching calls.

exercises.prompt: allow: `Bash(git *)`, deny: `Bash(git push *)`. Claude runs `git push origin main`. What happens?
options: It runs, because the allow rule is broader
It runs, because allow is listed first
exercises.explanation: Deny is always checked first and the first match wins, so a broad allow can never override a deny.

exercises.prompt: allow: `Bash(npm *)`, ask: `Bash(npm publish *)`. Claude runs `npm publish`. What happens?
options: Claude Code crashes on the conflict
exercises.explanation: Ask is checked before allow, so a matching ask rule always forces a confirmation even when an allow also matches.

exercises.prompt: Match each rule to its effect.
exercises.explanation: The same pattern behaves completely differently depending on which list it sits in, so placement matters as much as matching.

exercises.prompt: Why use a deny rule instead of writing "never read .env" in CLAUDE.md?
options: Deny rules are enforced by Claude Code; CLAUDE.md only guides the model
exercises.explanation: CLAUDE.md only guides what the model tries, while Claude Code itself enforces deny rules on every tool call.

exercises.prompt: Which rule matches exactly the same commands as `Bash(ls *)`?
exercises.explanation: The older `:*` suffix is just another way to write a trailing wildcard, so both rules match the same commands.

exercises.prompt: You need to guarantee Claude never reads your secrets. Which request is better?
options: Add a note to CLAUDE.md saying not to look at .env files.
Add Read(./.env) and Read(./.env.*) to the deny list in .claude/settings.json.
exercises.explanation: A deny rule is enforced by Claude Code every time, whereas a note can be overlooked by the model.

exercises.prompt: Make `git push` always ask first, and block `rm -rf` outright.
exercises.explanation: Putting `git push` in `ask` keeps you in the loop for pushes, while `deny` makes `rm -rf` impossible no matter what else is allowed.
exercises.hint: "ask" = confirm before running, "deny" = never run, "allow" = run without asking.

exercises.prompt: Put Claude Code's rule evaluation in order.
steps: No match: fall back to the current permission mode
exercises.explanation: Checking deny first makes blocks unbreakable, and the current mode only decides when no rule matches at all.

mission.title: Lock the Shell
mission.intro: Kip wants a safe tide pool. Set up modes and permission rules in a real repo.
checklist: Run `claude --permission-mode plan` in a real repo and ask for a plan for a small change
Press Shift+Tab a few times and watch the mode indicator change
Create `.claude/settings.json` with an allow rule for your test command and a deny rule for `Read(./.env)`
Run `/permissions` and confirm your rules appear with their source file
Ask Claude to read `.env` and watch the deny rule block it
mission.explanation: You now plan before editing and let enforced rules, not hope, guard your secrets.

cheatsheet.description: Cycle permission modes: Manual, accept edits, plan, and more.
Start a session in read-only plan mode.
Mode that auto-approves file edits and common filesystem commands.
View, add and remove allow, ask and deny rules.
Project settings, committed and shared with the team.
User settings for every project on your machine.
Rule evaluation order; the first match wins.
Rule matching any command starting with npm run.
Setting that picks the mode sessions start in.
Skip permission prompts. Only inside containers or VMs.
